sources.title: Smithsonian Contributions to Anthropology: Eastern Woodlands archaeological data and migration
sources.note: Scholarly regional synthesis maps shifting, spotty population concentrations and warns against treating intervening land as uniformly occupied territory.

sources.title: National Park Service: Woodland Culture at Ocmulgee
sources.note: Official site interpretation describes horticulture, settlements, art, exchange, and local Woodland developments before 900.

sources.title: National Park Service: documenting the Effigy Moundbuilders
sources.note: Official archaeology account dates regional effigy mounds, villages, mixed subsistence, gardens, wetlands, and culturally associated nations.

sources.title: National Park Service: Late Woodland life along the Upper Mississippi
sources.note: Official regional synthesis documents divergent Late Woodland economies, ceramics, horticulture, fishing, and limits on northern maize cultivation.

sources.title: Wisconsin Historical Society: Aztalan State Park
sources.note: State historical record describes a twenty-one-acre walled town, houses, hearths, mounds, fields, and archaeological interpretation.

sources.title: National Park Service: Mississippian Culture at Ocmulgee
sources.note: Official site account covers farming, storage, houses, mounds, pottery, textiles, games, social difference, and local change.

sources.title: Illinois Department of Natural Resources: Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site
sources.note: Official state site summary gives occupation, area, population range, mounds, stockade, and solar-alignment posts.

sources.title: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: ritual Black Drink at Cahokia
sources.note: Peer-reviewed residue study identifies Ilex biomarkers in Cahokian beakers dated 1050 to 1250 and explains analytical limits.

sources.title: University of Alabama: ancient Moundville site
sources.note: University museum account describes the town plan, palisade, plaza, mounds, occupation, transformation, and uncertain ethnic links.

sources.title: University of Alabama: Moundville self-guided tour
sources.note: Descendant-informed university guide distinguishes the modern Mississippian label and covers matrilineal clans, monuments, art, and continuity.

sources.title: Parks Canada: Droulers-Tsiionhiakwatha village
sources.note: Official backgrounder documents a mid-fifteenth-century St Lawrence Iroquoian village, structures, middens, tools, food remains, and preservation.

sources.title: Florida State Parks: Crystal River archaeology and history
sources.note: Official site history describes long coastal occupation, estuary-supported settlement, ceremonial change, and retained local identity.

sources.title: Royal Society Open Science: sleeping crops of eastern North America
sources.note: Peer-reviewed synthesis documents enduring Indigenous crop diversity, forest management, and continued native-crop cultivation alongside maize.

sources.title: Maryland Archaeological Conservation Laboratory: Shepard site
sources.note: State archaeology record documents a Potomac Late Woodland village, midden, animal bone, mussel shell, stone tools, and charred maize.

sources.title: National Park Service: life in northeast Florida around 1000
sources.note: Official evidence-based reconstruction describes marsh fisheries, oyster harvesting, fish weirs, crafts, council houses, and long-distance materials.

sources.title: National Park Service: Emerald Mound
sources.note: Official site account describes diverse Mississippian communities, mixed farming, game, fish, roots, nuts, berries, and ceremonial construction.

sources.title: Journal of Archaeological Science: immigrants at Cahokia
sources.note: Peer-reviewed strontium isotope study identifies nonlocal people, multiple origins, and movement often during late childhood or adolescence.

sources.title: Georgia State Parks: Etowah Indian Mounds
sources.note: Official state site describes a town, mounds, plaza, defensive ditch, farming, fishing, trade, craftsmanship, and medicinal plant interpretation.

sources.title: National Park Service: Werowocomoco
sources.note: Official tribal-partnered site account traces town development from about 1200, homes, crops, families, politics, ceremony, and trade.

sources.title: Oklahoma Historical Society: Spiro Mounds Archaeological Center
sources.note: Official site interpretation covers permanent settlement, trade, politics, ceremonial art, iconography, horticulture, looting, and descendant consultation.

sources.title: Smithsonian conservation research: Mississippian copper metalwork
sources.note: Museum conservation study documents hammering, thin sheeting, riveting, relief work, motifs, imaging, and workshop techniques.

sources.title: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Raleigh Island shell-bead workshops
sources.note: Peer-reviewed LiDAR and excavation study identifies a Florida shell-ring complex and intensive bead production from about 900 to 1200.

sources.title: National Park Service: Mississippian Culture at Russell Cave
sources.note: Official park interpretation covers shell-tempered pottery, farming, hunting, exchange, adornment, craft, and chunkey.

sources.title: University of Alabama Press: Archaeology of Everyday Life at Early Moundville
sources.note: University press summary reports multi-household groups, kin-like organization, feasts, risk sharing, autonomy, and domestic archaeological methods.

sources.title: Parks Canada: Southwold Earthworks culture
sources.note: Official site history documents a 1450 to 1550 palisaded village, longhouses, and extended families linked through maternal ancestry.

sources.title: New York State Museum: Mohawk Haudenosaunee longhouse
sources.note: State museum research explains extended-family longhouses, hearth groups, storage, smoke, building materials, and continuing Haudenosaunee meaning.

sources.title: Journal of Archaeological Science Reports: child fingernail impressions on Late Woodland pottery
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study tests childhood material interaction through fingernail impressions on fifteenth-century Ontario pottery.

sources.title: Western Journal of Medicine: health before Columbus
sources.note: Peer-reviewed paleopathology review explains skeletal limits and patterns in nutrition, infection, joints, women, and children.

sources.title: Smithsonian repository: Identification and paleopathology methods
sources.note: Smithsonian-hosted scholarly text explains that relatively few diseases leave visible skeletal change and that diagnoses retain multiple possibilities.

sources.title: Southeastern Archaeology: Late Cahokian subsistence and health
sources.note: University research record finds diverse Cahokian subpopulations with differing diets, dental evidence, health, and lifestyles.

sources.title: Archaeological Papers of the American Anthropological Association: Mississippian elite health
sources.note: Scholarly comparison finds varied and sometimes contradictory diet, disease, trauma, and status patterns across southeastern sites.

sources.title: National Park Service: Effigy Mounds Junior Ranger activity book
sources.note: Official educational guide summarizes seasonal villages, shelters, foods, pottery, ceremonies, ancestors, and locally used medicinal herbs.

sources.title: Illinois research: water and the emergence of Cahokia
sources.note: Peer-reviewed research record explains how wetland topography and natural and built water features shaped Cahokia spatially and symbolically.

sources.title: Maryland Archaeological Conservation Laboratory: Winslow site
sources.note: State archaeology record documents a circa-1300 palisaded village, refuse pits, household organization, maize, bone, shell, and tools.

sources.title: SUNY Fredonia research: excreta disposal at Angel Mounds
sources.note: Research preprint reports geochemical and microscopic evidence consistent with secondary human-waste disposal in one abandoned fourteenth-century house basin.

sources.title: Maryland Archaeological Conservation Laboratory: Harrison site
sources.note: State archaeology record dates Late Woodland shelter and shell midden deposits and identifies hunting, butchering, plant, fish, and hide work.

sources.title: Scientific Reports: drought during Cahokia abandonment
sources.note: Peer-reviewed lake-core study links persistent 1200 to 1400 drying with stress while preserving multicausal caution.

sources.title: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: flooding and Cahokia
sources.note: Peer-reviewed sediment-core study links reduced megaflood frequency with growth and renewed large floods with later decline.

sources.title: American Antiquity: Indigenous repopulation after Cahokia
sources.note: Peer-reviewed fecal-stanol reconstruction finds a regional low around 1400 and renewed Indigenous population by about 1500.

sources.title: Mississippi Department of Archives and History: Winterville Mounds
sources.note: State heritage account connects the site with Natchez ancestry and explains repeated community basket-load mound construction.

sources.title: University of Alabama: Jones Archaeological Museum
sources.note: Descendant-informed museum page identifies living Tribal partners, repatriation, and continuing artistic and cultural relationships.

sources.title: Parks Canada: Kejimkujik petroglyphs
sources.note: Official Mi’kmaw-partnered interpretation describes meaningful carvings before and after contact while leaving individual image dates unresolved.
